title: any, all and the walrus
summary: Express checks and searches in one line.

steps.title: any and all
body: `any(iterable)` is true if **some** item is truthy; `all(iterable)` if **every** item is. With a generator expression they read like LINQ's `Any` and `All`, and they stop early:
if any(n < 0 for n in nums):
if all(word.isalpha() for word in words):
Edge cases: `any([])` is `False`, `all([])` is `True` (nothing fails the test).

code: print(any(n % 2 for n in nums), all(n % 2 == 0 for n in nums))
print(all(len(w) > 2 for w in "the cat sat".split()))
steps.explain: `15 % 2` is 1, truthy, so `any` is true and `all(even)` false. Empty `all` is vacuously `True`.

steps.title: next with a default: find first
body: To find the first match (LINQ's `FirstOrDefault`), use `next` on a generator expression:
first_admin = next((u for u in users if u.is_admin), None)
It stops at the first match and returns `None` if there is none. No loop, no flag, no `break`.

steps.prompt: Which line returns the first word longer than 5 letters, or `""` if there is none?
options: `next((w for w in words if len(w) > 5), "")`
`[w for w in words if len(w) > 5][0]`
steps.explain: The list version raises `IndexError` when nothing matches and builds the whole list first. `any` returns a bool, not the word. A `filter` object cannot be indexed.

steps.title: The walrus operator
body: `:=` assigns **and** returns a value inside an expression. It shines when you would otherwise compute something twice:
cleaned = [y for x in data if (y := x.strip())]   # compute once, test and keep
It is like C#'s `if (dict.TryGetValue(k, out var v))` pattern: bind in the condition, use in the body. Do not use it just to save a line.

code: ids = [int(m.group(1)) for line in lines if (m := re.match(r"id=(\d+)", line))]
steps.explain: The walrus keeps the match object so it is not computed twice.

code: clean = [s for line in raw if (s __1__ line.strip())]
print(clean, __2__(s == "b" for s in clean))  # ['a', 'b'] True

steps.title: Password rules
prompt: Write `check_password(pw)` returning a list of the rules it **breaks**, in this order, or `[]` if it is fine:
Use `any` for each character test. Also write `first_weak(passwords)` returning the first password that breaks any rule, or `None`, using `next`.
solution: if not any(c.isdigit() for c in pw):
if not any(c.isupper() for c in pw):
if any(c.isspace() for c in pw):
return next((p for p in passwords if check_password(p)), None)
template: Dojo.eq("short, no digit, no upper", ["length", "digit", "upper"], check_password("abc"))
hints: `next((p for p in passwords if check_password(p)), None)`: a non-empty list is truthy.
